activities.title: Set design and development controls
activities.description: Determine whether design or development is part of the organization's responsibility and QMS scope, then establish proportionate controls where it applies. The method should connect needs to planned inputs, review points, verification, validation where relevant, approved outputs, changes, and retained decisions.
activities.objective: Establish a reviewed and traceable method for controlling design and development when the organization has that responsibility.
activities.why_it_matters: A factual applicability decision prevents both an invented design process and an unmanaged design responsibility.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Determine whether the organization designs or develops products, services, or outputs within its responsibility and scope.
2. If it applies, assign ownership and define inputs, stages, review points, verification, validation where relevant, outputs, and change controls.
3. Define how relevant functions or customers participate when their input is needed.
4. Define approval points and the decisions or results that need to be retained.
5. If it does not apply, record the factual business rationale through the existing control applicability and justification workflow.
6. Revisit the decision when responsibilities, offerings, customers, or operational context changes.
activities.expected_output: A proportionate design and development control method, or a reviewed applicability decision with documented rationale.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include a scope decision, design plan, input and output records, review decisions, verification or validation results, approved changes, and retained applicability rationale.
activities.success_criteria: The business-context decision is recorded, applicable design work has controlled inputs and outputs, review and verification are defined, changes are controlled, and non-applicability is never assumed by the system.
activities.responsible_role: Engineering / Design Owner with Quality Manager

activities.title: Define operational planning criteria
activities.description: Translate relevant requirements and QMS controls into practical conditions for performing and controlling operational work. Shape the method to the organization's products, services, resources, risks, and operating model.
activities.objective: Define the planning criteria that make operational results, responsibilities, resources, acceptance, monitoring, and records clear before work begins.
activities.why_it_matters: Useful planning criteria help people control quality in the real work context without forcing a manufacturing model onto a service organization.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify the products, services, or operational outputs being planned.
2. Define required results, responsibilities, resources, acceptance criteria, and relevant process controls.
3. Add monitoring points, records, and risk-based controls where they help maintain the intended result.
4. Describe how unusual, changed, or constrained conditions are handled.
5. Confirm the criteria are available to the people who plan and perform the work.
6. Review the planning method after meaningful changes or recurring issues.
activities.expected_output: Operational planning criteria that connect requirements, controls, resources, responsibilities, acceptance, monitoring, and records.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include an operational plan, service delivery plan, work order criteria, resource review, acceptance checklist, monitoring record, or exception decision.
activities.success_criteria: Operational work has usable criteria for the intended result, ownership and resources are clear, acceptance and monitoring are defined, and unusual conditions have a proportionate response.

activities.title: Control work instructions
activities.description: Determine where people need controlled operational guidance because complexity, risk, variation, competency, handoffs, history, or customer and regulatory needs could affect quality. Use the clearest practical format for the work.
activities.objective: Provide current and usable instructions where they materially support consistent quality results.
activities.why_it_matters: Focused instructions reduce avoidable variation while keeping the QMS useful instead of turning documentation into an end in itself.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify work where unclear guidance could affect quality, safety, delivery, or customer outcomes.
2. Consider complexity, risk, variation, competency, critical characteristics, handoffs, error history, and applicable obligations.
3. Decide where an instruction is needed and choose a suitable format such as an SOP, traveler, checklist, drawing, visual aid, workflow, setup sheet, or digital instruction.
4. Assign ownership and define review, approval, revision, access, and obsolete-information handling.
5. Check that the instruction is understandable and available at the point of use.
6. Review it when the work, tools, risks, or results materially change.
activities.expected_output: A risk-based set of controlled operational instructions in formats suited to the work, with clear review and point-of-use controls.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include an instruction decision, approved work aid, point-of-use check, revision history, obsolete-information record, or observation of use.
activities.success_criteria: Instruction needs are determined from the work context, formats fit the audience, current versions are available where needed, and unnecessary paperwork is avoided.

activities.title: Define verification and release controls
activities.description: Establish practical checks and an authorized release decision so products, services, or other outputs are not released before defined acceptance conditions are satisfied. Use controls at the points where they provide the most value.
activities.objective: Prevent premature release and retain enough result and approval information to show what was accepted.
activities.why_it_matters: Clear release controls protect customers from unintended results and make exceptions visible instead of accidental.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Define acceptance criteria for relevant products, services, or outputs.
2. Identify verification or review points throughout the work, not only at the end.
3. Assign the person or role authorized to decide release.
4. Define how status, result, approval, and retained release evidence are recorded when needed.
5. Define the response to unmet criteria and any controlled exception or deviation path that is permitted.
6. Review release controls after escapes, changes, or recurring acceptance issues.
activities.expected_output: Verification and release controls with acceptance criteria, authorized decisions, exception handling, and proportionate retained results.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include acceptance criteria, inspection or review records, release approval, status identification, exception approval, or a response to an unmet condition.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant acceptance conditions are known, checks occur at useful points, release authority is clear, unmet criteria are controlled, and release evidence is retrievable where needed.

activities.title: Establish identification and traceability
activities.description: Determine the identity and status information needed to control products, services, materials, work, or outputs. Choose a level of traceability that fits the nature of the work, risk, requirements, and ability to reconstruct history when necessary.
activities.objective: Maintain enough identity and history information to distinguish work and control its status throughout relevant operations.
activities.why_it_matters: Appropriate identification prevents mix-ups, supports status decisions, and enables focused investigation without imposing serial-level tracking everywhere.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify where confusion of product, service, material, work, or output status could affect quality.
2. Distinguish identification needs from the deeper history needed for traceability.
3. Choose practical identifiers such as part number, lot, batch, serial, job, order, traveler, service ticket, or system identifier where relevant.
4. Define status marking, linking, handoff, and record expectations.
5. Test whether selected records can reconstruct the needed history.
6. Reassess the level of traceability when risks, requirements, processes, or customer needs change.
activities.expected_output: An identification and traceability method proportionate to the organization's products, services, risks, and process needs.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include an identifier convention, status record, job history, lot or serial record, service ticket, handoff record, or traceability test.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant work has a clear identity and status, the selected traceability level is justified, handoffs remain understandable, and needed history can be reconstructed.

activities.title: Protect customer and external property
activities.description: Determine whether the organization controls property belonging to customers or other external parties, then define practical safeguards for the assets it receives, uses, stores, or accesses.
activities.objective: Protect entrusted physical, digital, intellectual, or other external property and communicate when it is lost, damaged, or unsuitable.
activities.why_it_matters: Clear handling of entrusted property protects customer interests and makes responsibility visible when something goes wrong.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Determine whether customer or external property is under the organization's control.
2. Identify relevant property such as material, tooling, equipment, data, drawings, credentials, access, or supplied information.
3. Define receipt, identification, verification where relevant, protection, access, use, storage, and return or disposition.
4. Define how loss, damage, mismatch, or suspected compromise is recorded and communicated.
5. If no relevant external property is controlled, record the factual applicability rationale through the existing workflow.
6. Review safeguards when the service, customer relationship, access model, or risk changes.
activities.expected_output: A proportionate external-property control method, or a reviewed applicability decision with rationale where no such property is controlled.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include receipt or inventory information, access approval, storage safeguard, condition check, incident record, customer notification, or applicability rationale.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant entrusted property is identified and protected, responsibilities and notifications are clear, and non-applicability is supported by facts rather than assumption.

activities.title: Establish preservation and handling controls
activities.description: Determine how products, materials, information, or service outputs need to be handled, stored, moved, protected, and delivered so their intended condition and usability are maintained.
activities.objective: Preserve quality through relevant handling, storage, movement, delivery, and service conditions.
activities.why_it_matters: Practical preservation controls protect results from avoidable damage, contamination, loss, deterioration, or digital integrity issues.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify outputs and conditions that could affect conformity or usability during operations, storage, movement, delivery, or service.
2. Determine relevant controls for handling, contamination, packaging, storage, environment, shelf life, segregation, transport, or digital integrity.
3. Set responsibilities, limits, checks, and response actions proportionate to risk.
4. Make necessary handling information available to the people and providers involved.
5. Review actual conditions and incidents for evidence that controls work.
6. Adjust the method when the output, route, environment, customer need, or risk changes.
activities.expected_output: Relevant preservation and handling controls with ownership, condition limits, checks, and response actions.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include handling instructions, storage condition record, packaging check, segregation marker, transport review, environmental check, or preservation incident.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant risks are identified, controls fit the output and route, responsibilities are clear, and the organization can respond when preservation conditions are not met.

activities.title: Control operational changes
activities.description: Create a proportionate method for evaluating planned and unplanned operational changes before they create uncontrolled quality risk. The method should cover impact, authorization, communication, verification, and controlled information.
activities.objective: Keep operational changes understood, authorized, communicated, and verified when their effect could matter to quality or customer outcomes.
activities.why_it_matters: A practical change method protects process results while avoiding unnecessary bureaucracy for routine minor adjustments.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Describe the proposed or actual change and why it is needed.
2. Assess effects on requirements, processes, documents, resources, people, suppliers, customers, and quality risks.
3. Define the required authorization and any verification or validation before use.
4. Communicate the change to affected people and providers.
5. Update controlled information and retain significant decisions or results.
6. Review the change after implementation when the impact or risk warrants follow-up.
activities.expected_output: A proportionate operational change control method with impact review, authorization, communication, and follow-up.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include a change request, impact review, approval, communication, updated work information, verification result, or post-change review.
activities.success_criteria: Material changes are described and evaluated, authority is appropriate, affected parties are informed, needed controls are updated, and routine minor adjustments remain proportionate.

activities.title: Capture customer requirements
activities.description: Establish a reliable intake method for understanding what the customer actually needs. Keep the method independent of any particular sales or commercial software and adapt it to the organization's products, services, and customer relationships.
activities.objective: Capture relevant customer requirements, clarifications, changes, and support expectations in a form the organization can use.
activities.why_it_matters: A dependable intake method reduces missed expectations and gives downstream teams a clear basis for planning and delivery.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify the relevant product or service, quantity or scope, timing, technical information, and acceptance needs.
2. Capture documentation, support, post-delivery, and change expectations where relevant.
3. Record questions, clarifications, assumptions, and decisions in the organization's existing order or service system.
4. Make the captured requirements available to the roles that plan, perform, review, and support the work.
5. Identify changes that require renewed review before they are used.
6. Review the intake method after misunderstandings, escapes, or recurring clarification needs.
activities.expected_output: A usable customer-requirements intake method with clear records, ownership, clarification, and change handling.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include an inquiry record, requirement summary, clarification decision, customer communication, change record, or handoff record.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant customer needs are captured and clarified, records reach affected roles, changes are visible, and the method works with the organization's existing tools.
activities.responsible_role: Customer Service / Sales Owner with Process Owners

activities.title: Review commitments before acceptance
activities.description: Evaluate whether the organization understands and can meet relevant commitments before accepting customer work. Keep this decision distinct from capturing the request: the request describes what is wanted, while this review evaluates capability and resolves differences.
activities.objective: Confirm requirement completeness, capability, resources, risks, dependencies, and authority before the organization accepts a commitment.
activities.why_it_matters: A timely capability review exposes differences and constraints before they become missed commitments or avoidable customer issues.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Review the captured requirements for completeness and clarity.
2. Compare them with the prior offer, quote, order, or agreed scope and resolve differences.
3. Evaluate capability, resources, capacity, technical feasibility, delivery, special risks, and supplier dependencies.
4. Record unresolved questions and define who can approve acceptance or conditions.
5. Communicate the accepted scope and any agreed limitations to affected roles.
6. Reopen the review when a material requirement or commitment changes.
activities.expected_output: A commitment-review method with capability evidence, resolved differences, approval authority, conditions, and change triggers.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include a pre-acceptance review, capability check, difference resolution, approval, conditional acceptance, supplier dependency review, or changed-commitment decision.
activities.success_criteria: Requirements are complete enough to decide, differences are resolved or controlled, capability and dependencies are considered, authority is clear, and changes trigger an appropriate review.
activities.responsible_role: Customer Service / Sales Owner with Operations Manager

activities.title: Qualify external providers
activities.description: Select and approve external providers using criteria suited to what they supply and the associated risk. Scale the depth of evaluation to criticality rather than applying one identical process to every provider.
activities.objective: Establish a risk-informed decision for selecting, approving, or conditionally approving providers that can affect quality or commitments.
activities.why_it_matters: Proportionate qualification focuses attention on provider capability and the controls that matter for the work.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify the supplied product, service, or process and its significance to quality and commitments.
2. Define evaluation criteria for capability, capacity, reliability, communication, and required controls.
3. Evaluate the provider using suitable information and record the rationale.
4. Approve, conditionally approve, or reject the provider and define controls or communication requirements.
5. Set review or reevaluation triggers for material changes, issues, or risk.
6. Use a factual applicability decision if the organization has little or no relevant external provision.
activities.expected_output: An external-provider qualification method with risk-based criteria, decision authority, approval rationale, and reevaluation triggers.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include provider evaluation, capability review, approval decision, conditions, required information, trial result, or reevaluation trigger.
activities.success_criteria: Provider significance and criteria are clear, evaluations support the decision, controls are communicated, approvals have rationale, and qualification depth is proportionate.
activities.responsible_role: Purchasing / Supply Chain Owner with Quality Manager

activities.title: Monitor supplier performance
activities.description: Maintain visibility of external-provider performance and act when it no longer supports requirements. Use monitoring methods and frequency that fit relevance, risk, history, and the type of provision.
activities.objective: Detect meaningful provider performance changes and trigger proportionate review or corrective action.
activities.why_it_matters: Ongoing visibility turns provider experience into timely decisions instead of allowing repeated defects, delays, or communication failures to accumulate.
activities.implementation_steps:
1. Identify provider performance signals relevant to the supplied product, service, or process.
2. Select practical measures such as quality, delivery, responsiveness, documentation, recurring issues, escapes, or corrective action.
3. Define review frequency and thresholds proportionate to risk and experience.
4. Review results and record exceptions, trends, decisions, or actions.
5. Escalate meaningful deterioration and reassess provider controls or approval when appropriate.
6. Adjust monitoring when provision, performance, customer needs, or risk changes.
activities.expected_output: A proportionate provider-performance monitoring method with measures, review triggers, decisions, and response actions.
activities.evidence_expectations: Examples may include an exception review, scorecard where useful, delivery or quality history, provider corrective action, periodic review, or risk-based reevaluation.
activities.success_criteria: Relevant performance is visible, review depth and timing are proportionate, deterioration prompts action, and monitoring remains distinct from the initial provider approval decision.
activities.responsible_role: Purchasing / Supply Chain Owner with Quality Manager
